doc.title: Bob Schulz interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Turk's love of Jelly Roll Morton and re-creating 1920s jazz
summary: Turk brought out Morton's music; 1920s jazz had substantial writing compared with later New Orleans groups.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Now those bands, I don’t know how many of them actually read music that much. If you’re saying that their music was pretty complicated, do you think it was worked out in rehearsals?
Well yeah. There are some things that were worked out. But I mean you had “Buddy’s Habits” and you had — the mind goes blank —

And Jelly Roll Morton, yeah. In fact Turk loved Jelly Roll Morton. He tried to bring out as much of the old Morton stuff as possible, and play as much of that as they could. And that music was going on back then. And that was the kind of music they wanted to re- create. A lot of the current New Orleans groups, although there’s some young guys down there now that are doing that, but in the 40s, 50s and 60s and 70s they were just playing things that were eight bars long, sixteen bars long, and just playing it. But that was the

music in those days, in the 20s. I mean that jazz was, the big name writers, I mean the Jelly Roll Mortons. Now they were writing and they were putting out some great stuff. So there was good music being played. And that’s what he wanted to re-create.
